mainTopic: The worry of crushed limbs (ריסוקי אברים): newborns, animals that fell, and birds that fell onto water or other surfaces
overview: The גמרא first asks whether the squeezing of birth might crush a newborn's limbs (ריסוקי אברים). It tries three proofs that there is no such worry. The first two are pushed off as cases of a caesarean birth (יוצא דופן). The third, about a בכור, cannot be a caesarean birth, so the גמרא explains it as a newborn that stood firmly on its legs. רב נחמן then rules that an animal thrown down in the slaughterhouse is not suspected of crushed limbs. A story about a bull that fell loudly backs this up with רב's teaching that a falling animal digs in its hooves. Next comes a fallen animal that got up: if it stood, it needs no 24-hour wait but needs בדיקה, and if it walked, the final הלכה is that it needs no בדיקה at all. The גמרא then asks where the בדיקה is done, and says the סימנין need no checking. Last, it turns to birds: one that fell onto water and swam by its own strength is fine, and a long list shows which landing surfaces are hard enough to raise a worry.

steps.title: Proof from a newborn baby who becomes impure through זיבה
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא says even a one-day-old baby becomes impure through זיבה. That would be impossible if every newborn were worried about crushed limbs.
steps.simpleTranslation: A newborn becomes impure through a זיבה discharge. If you thought a newborn has a worry of crushed limbs, the rule 'from his flesh, and not because of something forced on him' would apply here, and he would not become impure.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes quoting a ברייתא that started just before this point: even a one-day-old baby can become impure through זיבה. It uses this to prove that newborns are not worried about crushed limbs.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A זיבה discharge only makes someone impure if it comes 'from his flesh' on its own, not because of an outside cause like illness or injury. If birth crushed a baby's limbs, any discharge would be blamed on that injury and would not make him impure. Since the ברייתא says he does become impure, the גמרא concludes there is no worry of crushed limbs.

keyTerms.meaning: A gonorrhea-like discharge that can make a person impure
And if it would enter your mind (if you were to think)
Something forced on him, an outside cause beyond his control

phrases.english: becomes impure through a זיבה discharge,
phrases.notes: This is the end of a ברייתא that began just before here: even a baby one day old can become impure this way.

phrases.english: and if it should enter your mind
that he is subject to a worry of crushed limbs,
read here 'from his flesh'
and not because of something forced on him.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִי סָלְקָא דַעְתָּךְ יֵשׁ בּוֹ מִשּׁוּם רִיסּוּקֵי אֵבָרִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the proof the גמרא began just before this point.
steps.raayaObject: That a newborn has no worry of crushed limbs.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא saying a one-day-old baby becomes impure through זיבה, read together with the rule 'from his flesh, and not because of something forced on him'.

steps.title: Pushing off the proof: a caesarean birth
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא is talking about a baby born by caesarean, who was never squeezed through the birth canal.
steps.simpleTranslation: What are we dealing with here? A case where the baby came out through the side, by caesarean birth.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the proof. It says the ברייתא is only about a baby born through the mother's side, not through the birth canal.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The worry of crushed limbs comes from the squeezing of a normal birth. A caesarean baby was never squeezed, so his discharge really is 'from his flesh'. A normally born baby could still have the worry of crushed limbs.

keyTerms.meaning: What case are we dealing with here? (a way of narrowing a source to a specific case)
Born through the side wall of the belly (caesarean birth)

phrases.english: Here, what are we dealing with?
A case where he came out through the side.
phrases.notes: 'Through the side' means a caesarean birth, so the baby was never squeezed by labor.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof of step 1 by limiting the ברייתא to a narrow case.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Limits the ברייתא to a caesarean birth, so it says nothing about normal births.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The proof assumed the ברייתא was about any newborn, but it could be about one who was never squeezed by labor.

steps.title: Proof from a calf born on יום טוב
steps.stepSummary: A calf born on יום טוב may be slaughtered that same day, so apparently there is no worry of crushed limbs.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: a calf born on יום טוב may be slaughtered on that יום טוב.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a second ברייתא as a new proof. A calf born on יום טוב may be slaughtered and eaten right away.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If newborns had a worry of crushed limbs, we would have to wait 24 hours before slaughtering the calf, as we do for an animal that fell from a roof. Allowing it on the same day suggests there is no such worry.

phrases.english: Come and hear:
a calf that was born on a Festival,
one may slaughter it on the Festival.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּא שְׁמַע: עֵגֶל שֶׁנּוֹלַד בְּיוֹם טוֹב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: The first proof was pushed off, so the גמרא tries a second one.
steps.raayaObject: That a newborn animal has no worry of crushed limbs.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא allowing a calf born on יום טוב to be slaughtered that same day.

steps.title: Same answer: the calf was born by caesarean
steps.stepSummary: The calf ברייתא is also explained as a caesarean birth.
steps.simpleTranslation: Here too, it is a case where the calf came out through the side.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes off the second proof with the same answer it gave before.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A calf born by caesarean was never squeezed, so it can be slaughtered right away. A calf born normally might still need to wait 24 hours.

phrases.english: Here too,
it is a case where it came out through the side.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָכָא נָמֵי, כְּגוֹן שֶׁיָּצָא דֶּרֶךְ דּוֹפֶן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the answer of step 2 again to reject the proof of step 3.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Limits the calf ברייתא to a caesarean birth.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The ברייתא does not have to be about a normal birth.

steps.title: Proof from a בכור born with its blemish
steps.stepSummary: Everyone agrees that a בכור born on יום טוב with a blemish counts as prepared and may be eaten. So there is no 24-hour wait for crushed limbs.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: everyone agrees that if a firstborn animal was born together with its blemish, it counts as prepared for the Festival.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a third proof, about a בכור (firstborn animal) born on יום טוב already blemished. This step sets up a proof that the next step will defend.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A blemished בכור may be slaughtered and eaten. Since it was blemished from birth, it counts as מוכן (ready) for יום טוב and can be eaten that day. That only works if there is no worry of crushed limbs.

keyTerms.meaning: And all agree (even those who disagree elsewhere)
Its blemish, which allows a בכור to be eaten
Counted as prepared and ready for use on יום טוב

phrases.english: Come and hear:
and all agree that if it was born
phrases.notes: 'It' is a בכור, a firstborn animal, born on יום טוב.

phrases.english: it and its blemish with it,
phrases.notes: He means it already had the blemish when it was born.

phrases.english: that this is counted as prepared.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּא שְׁמַע: וְשָׁוִין שֶׁאִם נוֹלַד הוּא וּמוּמוֹ עִמּוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After two proofs were pushed off, the גמרא brings a third one.
steps.raayaObject: That a newborn animal has no worry of crushed limbs.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא saying a בכור born blemished on יום טוב counts as מוכן and may be eaten.

steps.title: The caesarean answer cannot work for a בכור
steps.stepSummary: You cannot say this ברייתא is about a caesarean birth, because a בכור born that way is not holy at all.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you would say here too that it came out through the side: is an animal that came out through the side holy? But רבי יוחנן said that רבי שמעון agreed, regarding holy animals, that such an animal is not holy!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא expects the usual answer, 'it was a caesarean birth', and shows it cannot work here. The ברייתא must be talking about a normal birth.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Only a normally born firstborn becomes a holy בכור. רבי יוחנן reports that even רבי שמעון agrees a caesarean animal is not holy as a קרבן. So the ברייתא's case has to be a normal birth, and the proof that there is no worry of crushed limbs stands.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you would say (bringing up a possible answer in order to reject it)
Holy animals, such as קרבנות and a בכור

steps.whatToRemember: The 'caesarean birth' answer pushed off the first two proofs, but it fails for a בכור. A caesarean animal is never a holy בכור, so the third ברייתא must be about a normal birth.
steps.confusionAlert: Here the גמרא is not rejecting a proof. It is rejecting a possible rejection, which makes the third proof stronger.

phrases.english: And if you would say, here too,
that it came out through the side,
is one born through the side holy?
But didn't רבי יוחנן say:
רבי שמעון would agree
regarding holy animals that it is not holy!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכִי תֵּימָא הָכָא נָמֵי שֶׁיָּצָא דֶּרֶךְ דּוֹפֶן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Blocks the step 2 and step 4 answer from being used against the step 5 proof.
steps.kashyaTarget: The possible answer that the בכור ברייתא is about a caesarean birth.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A caesarean animal is not a holy בכור (as רבי יוחנן reports about רבי שמעון), so the ברייתא cannot be about one.

steps.title: The firstborn stood firmly on the ground
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the ברייתא about the blemished בכור is talking about an animal that spread its legs on the ground and stood right after birth.
steps.simpleTranslation: The case here is a newborn that spread out its legs on the ground and stood up.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question from step 6 by explaining the case differently: the newborn בכור stood firmly on its legs right after birth.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 6 said we cannot explain the ברייתא as a caesarean birth, because then the animal would not be a holy בכור. So the גמרא says it was a normal birth, but the calf spread its legs and stood. That shows its limbs are fine, so there is no worry of crushed limbs and it may be eaten that day.

keyTerms.meaning: What case are we dealing with here? The גמרא uses this to limit a source to a specific situation.
Spread out its legs and stood on them

steps.confusionAlert: This answer does not say a normal birth never raises a worry of crushed limbs. It only removes the worry here because the animal clearly stood on its legs.

phrases.english: Here, what are we dealing with?
phrases.notes: He means the ברייתא about the blemished בכור born on יום טוב from step 5.

phrases.english: One that spread out its legs on the ground.
phrases.notes: The newborn stood up on its legs right away, which shows they were not crushed.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 6 by offering a new way to explain the case of the ברייתא.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the case (אוקימתא): a natural birth where the newborn stood firmly
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Without a caesarean explanation, the ברייתא would seem to prove that a newborn never has a worry of crushed limbs.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא is about a calf that stood on its legs, so it proves nothing about other newborns.

steps.title: No worry of crushed limbs in the slaughterhouse
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן rules that an animal thrown down in the slaughterhouse has no worry of crushed limbs.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן said: In the slaughterhouse there is no worry of crushed limbs.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new rule from רב נחמן: when animals are thrown down to be slaughtered, we do not worry that their limbs were crushed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Usually a hard fall can make an animal a טריפה through crushed limbs. But רב נחמן says an animal thrown down in the slaughterhouse is not suspected of this. The reason comes in step 11: a falling animal digs in its hooves until it reaches the ground.

keyTerms.meaning: Crushed or shattered limbs, which can make an animal a טריפה

phrases.english: And רב נחמן said: The slaughterhouse
phrases.notes: He means an animal thrown to the ground there to be slaughtered.

phrases.english: has no concern of crushed limbs.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the newborn animal to another case of crushed limbs: the slaughterhouse.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An animal thrown down in the slaughterhouse is not suspected of crushed limbs.

steps.title: The bull that fell and bellowed
steps.stepSummary: A bull fell loudly in the slaughterhouse, yet רב יצחק בר שמואל בר מרתא took its best portions without worry.
steps.simpleTranslation: A certain bull fell and its bellowing was heard. רב יצחק בר שמואל בר מרתא went in and took from the very best parts.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a story about a bull that fell hard in the slaughterhouse, and a sage who ate its meat anyway. This sets up the question in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The loud bellowing makes it sound like the fall was hard, which might worry us about crushed limbs. Still, the sage was not worried at all and took the choicest meat, which fits רב נחמן's rule.

phrases.english: A certain bull fell,
and the sound of its bellowing was heard,

phrases.aramaic: עָל רַב יִצְחָק בַּר שְׁמוּאֵל בַּר מָרְתָא
phrases.english: רב יצחק בר שמואל בר מרתא went in
and took from the very best portions.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A story that matches רב נחמן's slaughterhouse rule.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A sage ate from a bull that fell loudly in the slaughterhouse, showing no worry of crushed limbs.

steps.title: The רבנן ask for his source
steps.stepSummary: The Rabbis ask רב יצחק בר שמואל בר מרתא how he knew the bull was fine.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis said to him: From where do you know this?
steps.whatsHappening: The Rabbis ask the sage for his source, because the bull's loud fall seemed dangerous. This sets up his answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question is not an attack. They want to know what rule allowed him to ignore a fall that sounded so hard.

keyTerms.meaning: From where do you know this? A request for a source

phrases.english: The Rabbis said to him:
From where do you have this?

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמְרִי לֵיהּ רַבָּנַן מְנָא לָךְ הָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the reason behind the sage's action in the story.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The source that lets one ignore a hard-sounding fall in the slaughterhouse.

steps.title: The animal digs in its hooves as it falls
steps.stepSummary: He quotes רב: when falling, the animal digs in its hooves until it reaches the ground, so it lands safely.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to them: This is what רב said: It digs in its hooves until it reaches the ground.
steps.whatsHappening: The sage answers with a teaching of רב: a falling animal catches itself with its hooves, so it does not land hard.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even when it sounds bad, the animal brakes its fall by pressing its hooves into the ground. So the impact is softened and there is no real worry of crushed limbs. This explains why the slaughterhouse case is not a worry.
steps.whatToRemember: An animal thrown down in the slaughterhouse is not suspected of crushed limbs, because it catches itself with its hooves as it falls.

phrases.english: He said to them: This is what רב said:
It digs in its hooves until it reaches the ground.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the Rabbis' question.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: רב taught that a falling animal digs in its hooves until it reaches the ground, so its fall is softened.

steps.title: An animal that fell and then stood or walked
steps.stepSummary: רב rules that a fallen animal that stood up does not need a 24-hour wait but needs checking; if it walked, it does not even need checking.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה said in the name of רב: If it stood up, it does not need a 24-hour wait. Checking it certainly needs. If it walked, it does not need checking.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ruling of רב about an animal that fell and then got up, setting out different levels depending on what it did after the fall.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Standing up shows it is healthy enough that we need not wait 24 hours, but we still check its body after שחיטה for damage. Walking is a stronger sign of health, so רב says no checking is needed at all.

keyTerms.meaning: Checking the animal's insides after שחיטה for damage

phrases.english: רב יהודה said in the name of רב:
If it stood up, it does not need a 24-hour wait,
but checking it certainly needs,
if it walked, it does not need checking.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on to a new rule about animals that fell and then got up.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Stood up: no 24-hour wait but needs checking. Walked: no checking needed.

steps.title: Even if it walked, it needs checking
steps.stepSummary: רב חייא בר אשי disagrees and says both an animal that stood and one that walked need checking.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חייא בר אשי said: Both this one and that one need checking.
steps.whatsHappening: רב חייא בר אשי gives a different opinion: walking after the fall is not enough, and the animal still has to be checked.
steps.deeperAnalysis: He agrees with רב that standing up needs checking. But he disagrees about walking: to him, walking does not prove there is no hidden damage, so checking is always required.

keyTerms.meaning: Both this one and that one

steps.whatToRemember: Both agree that an animal which fell and stood up needs checking. They argue about one that walked: רב says no checking, רב חייא בר אשי says checking is still needed.

phrases.english: רב חייא בר אשי said:

phrases.aramaic: אַחַת זוֹ וְאַחַת זוֹ צְרִיכָה בְּדִיקָה.
phrases.english: Both this one and that one need checking.
phrases.notes: He means both the animal that only stood and the one that also walked.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Disagrees with רב's ruling in step 12 about the animal that walked.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An animal that fell needs checking after שחיטה whether it stood or walked.

steps.title: Starting to stand or walk already counts
steps.stepSummary: רב ירמיה בר אחא quotes רב: if the animal stretched its foreleg to stand, it counts as standing. If it lifted its leg to walk, it counts as walking.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב ירמיה בר אחא said in the name of רב: if the animal stretched out its foreleg to stand, it counts even if it did not actually stand. If it lifted its leg to walk, it counts even if it did not actually walk.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains how much 'standing' and 'walking' an animal needs for רב's rule from Step 12 to apply.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In Step 12, רב said that standing removes the 24-hour wait and walking removes the need for בדיקה. Here we learn that a real attempt is enough. Stretching the foreleg counts as standing, and lifting a leg to walk counts as walking.

keyTerms.meaning: It lifted (uprooted) its leg from the ground

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב יִרְמְיָה בַּר אַחָא אָמַר רַב:
phrases.english: Rav Yirmeya bar Acha said that Rav said:
If it stretched out its foreleg to stand,
even though it did not stand, it counts as standing.
If it lifted its leg to walk,
even though it did not walk, it counts as walking.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב יִרְמְיָה בַּר אַחָא אָמַר רַב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Defines the terms 'stood' and 'walked' from רב's ruling in Step 12.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An attempt to stand counts as standing, and an attempt to walk counts as walking.

steps.title: Even struggling to stand counts
steps.stepSummary: רב חסדא is more lenient: if the animal just struggled to get up, it counts as having stood.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חסדא said: if the animal struggled to stand, it counts even though it did not stand.
steps.whatsHappening: רב חסדא gives an even easier standard for what counts as 'standing'.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב needed the animal to stretch out its foreleg. רב חסדא says that even shaking itself and straining to rise is enough to count as standing.

keyTerms.meaning: It stirred or struggled (shook itself) to get up

phrases.english: And Rav Chisda said:
If it struggled to stand,
even though it did not stand, it counts as standing.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a more lenient definition of 'standing' than רב in Step 14.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Struggling to rise is already considered standing.

steps.title: The final ruling for an animal that fell from a roof
steps.stepSummary: The הלכה: an animal that fell from a roof without meaning to, and stood but did not walk, needs בדיקה but no 24-hour wait. If it walked, it does not even need בדיקה.
steps.simpleTranslation: The הלכה is: when an animal fell off a roof without knowing, then stood up but did not walk, it needs checking but does not need a 24-hour wait. If it walked, it does not even need checking.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the final practical ruling for a fallen animal.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ruling matches רב's position from Step 12 against רב חייא בר אשי from Step 13: walking removes the need for בדיקה. It also states the case clearly: an accidental fall from a roof.
steps.whatToRemember: Stood only: check it after שחיטה, but you may slaughter right away. Stood and walked: no check needed at all.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is the practical הלכה for a fallen animal, and it settles the argument in Steps 12–13.

phrases.english: And the halacha is: where it fell from the roof
without knowing,
and it stood but did not walk —
it needs checking,
but it does not need a 24-hour wait.
And if it walked —
it does not even need checking.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Settles the argument between רב and רב חייא בר אשי.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Fell by accident and stood: בדיקה but no wait. Walked: no בדיקה.

steps.title: Check the area of the intestines
steps.stepSummary: אמימר quotes רב דימי of נהרדעא: the בדיקה for a fallen animal is done around the intestines.
steps.simpleTranslation: אמימר said in the name of רב דימי of נהרדעא: the fallen animal that needs checking must be checked around the intestines.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now asks a new practical question: where exactly is the בדיקה done?
steps.deeperAnalysis: We already know that some fallen animals need checking. אמימר says the checking is focused on the intestines, since that is where he expects damage from a fall.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר אַמֵּימָר מִשְּׁמֵיהּ דְּרַב דִּימִי מִנְּהַרְדְּעָא:
phrases.english: Ameimar said in the name of Rav Dimi of Neharde'a:
The fallen animal that they said needs checking
is checked around the intestines.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר אַמֵּימָר מִשְּׁמֵיהּ דְּרַב דִּימִי מִנְּהַרְדְּעָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on the requirement of בדיקה and asks where it is done.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The בדיקה of a נפולה is around the intestines.

steps.title: Check the whole body cavity
steps.stepSummary: מר זוטרא reports a different version in the name of רב פפא: the entire body cavity must be checked.
steps.simpleTranslation: מר זוטרא said to him: this is what we say in the name of רב פפא: it must be checked around the whole body cavity.
steps.whatsHappening: מר זוטרא answers אמימר with a different, wider tradition about where the checking is done.
steps.deeperAnalysis: אמימר limited the check to the intestines. מר זוטרא's tradition requires checking the entire בית החלל, which is a broader and stricter demand.

keyTerms.meaning: This is how we say it (a different tradition)
The body cavity, the hollow inside the body

phrases.english: Mar Zutra said to him:
This is what we say in the name of Rav Pappa:
It needs checking
around the entire body cavity.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ מָר זוּטְרָא הָכִי אָמְרִינַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Disagrees with אמימר's narrower tradition.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The whole body cavity must be checked.

steps.title: Do the windpipe and gullet need checking?
steps.stepSummary: הונא מר, the grandson of רב נחמיה, asks רב אשי whether the סימנין also need checking after a fall.
steps.simpleTranslation: הונא מר, the grandson of רב נחמיה, said to רב אשי: what about the סימנין?
steps.whatsHappening: A new question comes up about another body part, the סימנין, and whether they need checking.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The discussion so far covered the area inside the body. Now he asks whether the windpipe and food pipe, which sit outside that cavity, also need inspection.

keyTerms.meaning: The windpipe and food pipe, which are cut in שחיטה

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ הוּנָא מָר בַּר בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב נְחֶמְיָה לְרַב אָשֵׁי:
phrases.english: Huna Mar, the grandson of Rav Nechemya, said to Rav Ashi:
What about the simanim? Do they need checking?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Extends the question of where to check to include the סימנין.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether the סימנין of a fallen animal need בדיקה.

steps.title: The סימנין are tough and don't need checking
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי answers that the סימנין are hard and hold up in a fall, so they do not need checking.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: the סימנין are tough when it comes to falling.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי answers the question: there is no need to check the סימנין.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The reason is physical. The windpipe and gullet are strong, so a fall does not damage them, and we have no reason to worry about them.
steps.whatToRemember: After a fall, check inside the body (the intestines or the whole cavity, depending on the version). The סימנין do not need checking because they are tough.

phrases.english: He said to him:
The simanim are tough when it comes to falling.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers הונא מר's question.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The סימנין need no בדיקה because a fall does not damage them.

steps.title: A bird that fell onto water and swam is fine
steps.stepSummary: שמואל rules that a bird that fell onto water and then swam the length of its own body needs nothing more.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה says in the name of שמואל: if a bird was knocked down onto the water, once it swims its full body-length, that is enough.
steps.whatsHappening: שמואל moves from an animal that fell to a bird that fell onto water. He says swimming a body-length shows the bird is fine.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For an animal, walking after a fall showed its limbs were not crushed (step 16). For a bird in water, swimming its own length does the same job. So no בדיקה is needed.

keyTerms.meaning: was knocked down, fell with force

phrases.english: Rav Yehuda says that Shmuel says:
A bird that was knocked down onto the surface of the water,
once it swims the full length of its body – that is enough.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Extends the fallen-animal rules to a bird that fell onto water.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A bird that fell onto water and swam its full body-length needs no further concern.

steps.title: Only swimming upstream counts
steps.stepSummary: The rule only works if the bird swam upstream; swimming downstream proves nothing.
steps.simpleTranslation: We only said this when it swam upstream. Downstream, it was just the water carrying it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא limits שמואל's rule: the swimming has to be upstream.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The swim only proves something if the bird moved by its own strength. Going downstream, the current could be doing all the work. So downstream movement does not show the bird is healthy.

phrases.english: And we said this only from below to above,
phrases.notes: He means swimming upstream, against the current.

phrases.english: but from above to below –
it is the water that carried it down.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Narrows שמואל's rule to upstream swimming.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Only upstream swimming proves the bird is fine; downstream swimming does not.

steps.title: Standing water, and overtaking floating straw
steps.stepSummary: In still water, any swimming counts. Even downstream, if the bird passes straw floating in the current, it counts too.
steps.simpleTranslation: If the water is still, there is no problem. If straw was thrown in and the bird got ahead of it, then it clearly got ahead by itself.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds two cases where swimming does count: still water, and passing floating straw.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both cases answer the same worry from step 22: was the water moving the bird? In still water there is no current at all. If the bird passes straw that is drifting with the current, it must be moving faster than the water, so it is using its own strength.

keyTerms.meaning: we have no problem with it

phrases.aramaic: וְאִי מַיָּא קָיְימִי – לֵית לַן בַּהּ,
phrases.english: And if the water is standing – we have no problem with it,
and if one threw down straw and it overtook it –
phrases.notes: This is still talking about a bird swimming downstream.

phrases.english: look, it overtook it.

steps.whatToRemember: The real test is whether the bird moved by its own strength, more than the current could carry it.
steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִי מַיָּא קָיְימִי – לֵית לַן בַּהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives cases where the downstream worry does not apply.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Swimming in still water, or passing floating straw, shows the bird moved by itself.

steps.title: Falling onto a garment or a net
steps.stepSummary: A tight garment or a net with close knots is a hard landing, so we worry. Loose or folded cloth, or a net with knots far apart, is soft, so we don't.
steps.simpleTranslation: A tight garment: we worry. Not tight: we don't. Folded: we don't. A net with close knots: we worry. Knots not close: we don't.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a list of surfaces a bird might fall onto, and says whether each one makes us worry. This step covers garments and nets.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question each time is whether the surface is hard enough to crush the bird's limbs. Stretched cloth and tight netting don't give way, so they can hurt. Loose or folded cloth and wide netting do give way, so they soften the fall.

keyTerms.meaning: we are concerned (so the bird needs checking)

steps.confusionAlert: חָיְישִׁינַן does not mean the bird is automatically טרפה. It means there is a real worry, so we cannot simply assume the bird is fine.

phrases.english: A taut garment – we are concerned;
one that is not taut – we are not concerned;
folded over and over – we are not concerned;
a net whose knots are close together – we are concerned;
if the knots are not close together – we are not concerned.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from falling onto water to falling onto different surfaces.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Tight cloth and close-knotted nets raise concern; loose or folded cloth and loose nets do not.

steps.title: Falling onto bundles of flax or reeds
steps.stepSummary: Landing right on bundled flax or reed bundles is a hard landing, so we worry. Landing beside the bundles, we don't.
steps.simpleTranslation: Flax tied into bundles: we worry. This side or that side of them: we don't. Bundles of reeds: we worry.
steps.whatsHappening: The list goes on with flax and reeds that have been tied into bundles.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Tied bundles are packed tight and hard, so a bird landing directly on them could be crushed. Landing at the sides, the fall is softened and no worry is needed.

phrases.english: Flax that was made into bundles – we are concerned;

phrases.aramaic: דְּהַאי גִּיסָא וּדְהַאי גִּיסָא – לָא חָיְישִׁינַן;
phrases.english: on this side or on that side – we are not concerned;
phrases.notes: He means the bird landed beside the bundles instead of right on top of them.

phrases.english: bundles of reeds – we are concerned;

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the list of surfaces.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Landing right on hard bundles of flax or reeds raises concern; landing beside them does not.

steps.title: Different stages of processed flax
steps.stepSummary: Flax that is beaten and combed is soft. Flax that is not combed, or is tied with knots, or is coarse tow, is hard. Fine tow is soft.
steps.simpleTranslation: Flax beaten and combed: no worry. Beaten but not combed: worry. Made into bundles, since it has knots: worry. Coarse tow: worry. Fine tow: no worry.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes through flax at different stages of processing and decides which ones are soft enough to land on safely.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Combing removes the hard bits, so combed flax is soft. Uncombed flax still has hard stalk pieces. Even combed flax becomes hard again if it is tied into knotted bundles. Coarse tow is rough, while fine tow is soft.

phrases.english: Flax that is beaten and combed – we are not concerned;
beaten but not combed – we are concerned;
flax that was made into bundles,
since there are knots in it – we are concerned;
tow – we are concerned;
fine tow – we are not concerned.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the flax cases, now by stage of processing.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Soft flax (combed, or fine tow) raises no concern; hard flax (uncombed, knotted, or coarse tow) does.

steps.title: Palm fibers, palm bark, and ashes
steps.stepSummary: Palm fibers and sifted ashes are hard, so we worry. Strips of palm bark and unsifted ashes are soft, so we don't.
steps.simpleTranslation: Palm fibers: worry. Palm bark strips: no worry. Sifted ashes: worry. Unsifted: no worry.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes the list with palm materials and ashes.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here too, the only question is how hard the landing surface is. Sifted ashes pack down firm, while unsifted ashes scatter when something hits them and soften the fall.

keyTerms.meaning: the fibers that grow around a palm tree

steps.whatToRemember: The whole list follows one idea: a hard, firm surface means we worry about crushed limbs, and a soft surface that gives way means we don't.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that the worry about a bird that fell depends on what it landed on, not just on the fact that it fell.

phrases.english: Palm fibers – we are concerned;
palm bark strips – we are not concerned;
sifted ashes – we are concerned;
unsifted – we are not concerned.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the list of landing surfaces.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Palm fibers and sifted ashes raise concern; palm bark strips and unsifted ashes do not.
